candidato.titulo: Two omicron variants replicate more efficiently in gut tissue models, experiments reveal
candidato.resumo: A research team from the School of Public Health at the LKS Faculty of Medicine, the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), has discovered that emerging omicron sublineages of SARS-CoV-2 use distinct biological strategies to spread and cause disease. Specifically, the XBB.1.5 and EG.5.1 variants are better adapted for respiratory spread and may pose a heightened risk of severe respiratory disease, while BA.2.86 and JN.1 tend to replicate more effectively in the intestines, potentially opening alternative transmission routes.

texto_fonte:
Two omicron variants replicate more efficiently in gut tissue models, experiments reveal
A research team from the School of Public Health at the LKS Faculty of Medicine, the University of Hong Kong (HKUMed), has discovered that emerging omicron sublineages of SARS-CoV-2 use distinct biological strategies to spread and cause disease. Specifically, the XBB.1.5 and EG.5.1 variants are better adapted for respiratory spread and may pose a heightened risk of severe respiratory disease, while BA.2.86 and JN.1 tend to replicate more effectively in the intestines, potentially opening alternative transmission routes.
This research highlights the importance of ongoing monitoring and functional characterization of emerging strains to support public health planning and preparedness for future outbreaks. The findings were published in Nature Communications.
Since the emergence of omicron variants, SARS-CoV-2 has continued to evolve into numerous sublineages. Scientists have found it increasingly difficult to determine whether differences in transmission and disease severity are caused by the virus itself or by existing immunity built up through vaccination or previous infections.
To address this, the researchers conducted controlled laboratory experiments using models that closely mimic human tissues, including human bronchial and lung tissues, airway organoids (miniature lab-grown models that resemble the human airway), and intestinal models, including proximal intestinal enteroids (miniature models of the small intestine) and colon cells.
The researchers directly compared the intrinsic biological properties of omicron variants ranging from BA.1 to JN.1 under the same experimental conditions to better understand their differences in infection, replication and transmission potential.
Four sublineages infecting respiratory tissues may increase risk of severe lung disease
The study found that several omicron sublineages, including BA.5, BA.5.2.1, XBB.1.5 and EG.5.1, replicated efficiently in human respiratory tissues. This suggests that these variants are particularly effective at infecting and multiplying in the airways and lungs, which may facilitate person-to-person transmission and potentially increase the risk of severe lung disease. Among the variants studied, EG.5.1 showed particularly notable features.
Professor Michael Chan Chi-wai, from the School of Public Health, HKUMed, said, "EG.5.1 can enter human cells through two different pathways, making it easier to infect tissues. It also showed enhanced growth in alveolar epithelial cells, which are located deep in the lungs, suggesting a stronger ability to infect the lower respiratory system and potentially causing more serious illnesses."
The researchers observed a similar pattern in XBB.1.5, which also replicated efficiently in respiratory tissues, indicating a high level of transmissibility.
JN.1 intestinal adaptation points to potential fecal transmission pathway
The study found that BA.2.86 and JN.1, in contrast, replicated less efficiently than EG.5.1 in respiratory tissues but demonstrated higher replication levels in proximal intestinal enteroids, suggesting that they are better adapted to infect and grow in certain parts of the intestine. Interestingly, this increased replication was not observed in colon cells, indicating that the virus may prefer specific regions within the intestines.
Another important finding is that JN.1 exhibits a stronger ability to infect and grow in gut tissues while triggering relatively low levels of inflammation. This combination suggests that the virus may persist in the gut without causing obvious symptoms, potentially increasing the possibility of transmission through fecal contamination.
Chan commented, "The study highlights that while some variants are optimized for respiratory spread, others may be evolving to survive and multiply better in the gastrointestinal tract, which could influence how the virus spreads. The research also provides practical insights for laboratory studies, demonstrating that airway organoids are more reliable for studying how SARS-CoV-2 enters and infects human cells.
"The findings also suggest that the proximal intestine may be more relevant than the colon when investigating potential fecal transmission."
The study emphasizes that SARS-CoV-2 continues to evolve along different biological pathways, which could enable alternative transmission routes.
Chan explained, "Since new variants can develop from existing lineages, like BA.2.86 and JN.1 evolving from BA.2, it is very important to continue to monitor and study these emerging strains. As immunity from vaccinations and previous infections can decline over time, understanding how these viruses evolve and behave will help inform public health planning and strengthen preparedness for future outbreaks."
Publication details
Kenrie PY Hui et al., SARS-CoV-2 Omicron BA.2.86 and JN.1 expand tropism in human proximal intestinal epithelium, Nature Communications (2026). DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74111-y
Journal information: Nature Communications

candidato.titulo: Noise-cancelling headphones prevent vomiting after surgery
candidato.resumo: Nausea and vomiting are common after surgery, which may be partly related to the noises patients are exposed to, even under general anaesthetic. Wearing noise-cancelling headphones while on the operating table reduces the risk

texto_fonte:
Nausea and vomiting are common after surgery, but wearing noise-cancelling headphones during the procedure helps prevent these unpleasant side effects. This simple intervention also supports the idea that our brain processes sounds even when we’re not consciously aware of our surroundings.
“That data is really encouraging and is actually in line with decades of research showing that anaesthesia is not simply an off switch,” says Vigi Katlowitz at the Baylor College of Medicine in Houston.
Nausea and vomiting are common side effects of anaesthetics. Patients are routinely given drugs to prevent them, but Huayue Liu at the First Affiliated Hospital of Soochow University in Suzhou, China, and his colleagues wanted to investigate a non-pharmacological approach and presented their results at the Anesthesiology conference in San Diego.
Advertisement
The team recruited 192 patients who had keyhole gynaecological surgery under general anaesthesic. Half were randomly assigned noise-blocking ear defenders, which they wore from the start of anaesthesia until the end of surgery. All the patients received standard anaesthesia and anti-nausea medication.
Within 48 hours of the surgery, 35 per cent of those wearing ear defenders experienced nausea or vomiting, compared with 52 per cent of those without them. The researchers also found that symptoms were less severe among those whose hearing had been protected, defined as the patients vomiting less and it having less of an impact on their daily life.
Operating theatres aren’t generally quiet places, with Liu recording average noise levels of 66 decibels – around the level of a normal conversation – during the study.
The relationship between sound, nausea and vomiting, and anaesthesia is unclear. However, the latter affects the nervous system, and noise is thought to trigger a stress response that activates the autonomic nervous system. This helps regulate involuntary bodily functions, such as heart rate, and interacts with the brainstem pathways involved in nausea and vomiting.
However, Liu stresses that the researchers didn’t look into the mechanism behind how ear defenders prevent nausea and vomiting, so the idea of them dampening this response “remains a hypothesis”.
Nevertheless, the results tell us more about brain activity under anaesthesia. “The biological plausibility is that general anaesthesia produces unconsciousness without necessarily eliminating all neural processing of sound,” says Liu.
Liu hopes to one day conduct a larger trial at multiple locations that measures noise exposure relative to nervous system activity among patients under general anaesthetic.

candidato.titulo: How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots
candidato.resumo: Several factors, from sensors to safety and robotic arms or mobile platforms, help determine the selection of a brushless DC or BLDC motor. The post How to choose a BLDC motor for robotic arms and mobile robots appeared first on The Robot Report .

texto_fonte:
Selecting a brushless DC, or BLDC, motor for robotic arms or mobile robots starts with the mechanical system, not the controller catalog. A motor rated for a particular voltage and wattage does not tell an engineer whether it can deliver the required torque at low speed, regulate position accurately, absorb regenerative energy, or survive the thermal duty cycle.
The actuator is a system. The motor, inverter, current sensors, rotor position feedback, gearbox, brake, output encoder, thermal path, communications interface, and higher level robot software all influence the result.
An industrial or collaborative robotic arm joint generally prioritizes controllable torque, low-speed smoothness, position accuracy, collision response, backdrivability, and thermal performance. A mobile robot drive motor generally puts more emphasis on efficiency, starting torque, braking, traction, battery utilization, speed regulation, and synchronization between drive channels.
The terminology also deserves care. Commercial robotics literature often uses “BLDC” and “PMSM” (permanent magnet synchronous motor) somewhat interchangeably because both are three-phase, permanent-magnet machines driven by electronic inverters. Their back EMF waveform, winding design, controller algorithm, and feedback method still determine how a particular motor behaves.
For example, STMicroelectromics treats three-phase BLDC and PMSM control as related application areas and describes both six-step and field-oriented control architectures.
Start with the mechanical load, not the controller catalog
The first selection exercise is to establish what the motor actually has to do. For a geared robotic joint, a useful first order relationship is: τ_joint = (τ_motor × gear ratio × η_gear) − τ_losses
Motor speed follows the transmission ratio: ω_motor = ω_joint × gear ratio
Mechanical power is: P_mech = τ × ω
And a first approximation of battery side electrical power is: P_elec ≈ P_mech / η_total
These equations do not replace a dynamic model, but they expose the parameters that matter before a controller is selected. Considerations include continuous torque, peak torque, peak duration, acceleration torque, gravity torque, and reflected inertia. In addition, regenerative braking, stall or near stall operation, duty cycle, thermal resistance, battery voltage range, and cable and connector current limits should all be established.
For robotic arms, the load calculation has to account for link inertia, payload, gravity compensation, gearbox ratio, backlash, compliance, counterbalance, and encoder location. A motor side encoder can report the rotor position accurately while the joint output still contains transmission error.
For mobile robots, the equivalent exercise starts with vehicle mass, wheel radius, rolling resistance, slope, acceleration, terrain, wheel slip, and drive configuration. Differential-drive platforms impose different synchronization requirements from four wheel drive vehicles. An outdoor uncrewed ground vehicle (UGV) can also spend much more time in high load operation than a lightweight indoor delivery robot.
Regenerative energy deserves particular attention. During deceleration or downhill travel, the motor can return energy to the DC bus. The battery, controller, braking strategy, and bus capacitance all have to accommodate that energy. A controller that handles acceleration correctly can still create an over-voltage problem during aggressive regenerative braking.
Choose the commutation method according to motion quality
Six-step, sinusoidal, and field-oriented controls are not interchangeable labels for the same behavior.
Six-step, or trapezoidal, commutation switches the inverter through six electrical states according to rotor position. It can be attractive where implementation simplicity and cost matter or torque ripple is acceptable. It can also be suitable when the motor spends much of its operating time at moderate or high speed and precise low speed torque is not a central requirement. Hall sensors can provide the rotor position information needed for straightforward sensored implementations.
Sinusoidal control drives the phases with continuously varying current or voltage references rather than the discrete commutation states associated with basic six-step operation. It can reduce torque ripple and acoustic effects compared with a simple trapezoidal strategy, although actual performance depends on motor construction, feedback, current regulation, and tuning.
Field-oriented control, or FOC, takes the control problem further by transforming the measured phase currents into a rotating reference frame. The Clarke transformation converts the three phase quantities into a stationary two-axis representation, while the Park transformation rotates that representation into d axis and q axis components.
The controller can then regulate the components independently through current loops before transforming the command back into phase voltages and generating pulse width modulation (PWM).
In a typical PMSM application, q axis current is closely associated with torque production, while d axis current can be used for flux related control and, at higher speeds, field weakening. TI‘s motor control reference material illustrates the practical structure with Clarke and Park transformations, PI regulators, position and speed loops, and space vector PWM.
FOC is commonly attractive when the application requires smooth low-speed motion, fast torque response, or accurate speed regulation. It can also help with reduced torque ripple, regenerative braking, field weakening, or torque control for impedance and force-related behavior. FOC can therefore be a natural fit for many robotic joint and traction applications.
FOC does not automatically create a precision actuator. Rotor angle accuracy, current sense quality, motor parameter identification, sampling timing, inverter dead time, loop bandwidth, mechanical transmission, and tuning all affect the final result. A highly sophisticated algorithm cannot compensate for an encoder that is incorrectly aligned or a gearbox with substantial mechanical error.
Select the feedback architecture
Feedback selection is as important as the commutation algorithm. Hall effect sensors, incremental encoders, absolute magnetic encoders, optical encoders, resolvers, and sensorless estimation each solve different problems.
Hall sensors provide relatively coarse rotor position information and are often adequate for electronic commutation and basic speed control. They can be practical for cost-sensitive mobile platforms where the control objective does not require fine position information.
Incremental encoders provide substantially more position information and are widely used for servo control. Absolute encoders add an unambiguous position reference, which can be valuable when a robot has to know joint position immediately after startup without performing a homing sequence.
Optical encoders can provide high resolution but require appropriate mechanical and environmental protection. Magnetic encoders can offer compact packaging and tolerance for some contamination environments. Resolvers remain relevant where electrical and mechanical robustness are important.
The location of the sensor is just as important as its resolution. A motor-side encoder measures motor position. With a reduction gearbox, the output position also depends on gear ratio, backlash, compliance, torsional windup, bearing deformation, and transmission error. If those errors materially affect the task, an output side encoder can close the control loop around the actual joint position.
That does not mean every robot joint requires dual encoders. The mechanical transmission determines whether motor-side feedback provides sufficient accuracy. The Robot Report has previously covered actuator architectures using integrated servo drives and dual absolute encoders, illustrating why encoder placement becomes a system-level design issue as actuator size and performance requirements increase.
Sensorless BLDC control eliminates position sensors and their wiring, reducing cost and packaging complexity. Back EMF-based methods are established engineering techniques, and Microchip documents several implementations. The limitation is that back EMF information becomes difficult to obtain at zero and very low speed, so startup and heavily loaded low-speed operation require an appropriate strategy.
Sensorless control can therefore be useful in applications where the operating profile gives the estimator enough information, but it should not be treated as universally appropriate or inappropriate.
Match the controller to the robotic arm
A simple robotic arm joint can use a BLDC motor with Hall sensors and an external controller when the application mainly requires speed or basic position control and can tolerate relatively coarse rotor feedback. This architecture can be straightforward to commission and service, but the achievable motion quality depends heavily on the motor, gearbox, sensor resolution, controller capabilities, and higher level feedback.
A more demanding robotic joint commonly uses a BLDC or PMSM with an encoder based FOC servo drive. The drive can run a fast current loop locally, with velocity and position loops layered above it. The robot controller then commands the desired operating variable while the servo drive handles the high speed electrical control.
This architecture makes torque control practical and provides a foundation for position, velocity, impedance, and collision response strategies. Commissioning also becomes more involved. Encoder alignment, direction, current sense polarity, current loop tuning, velocity loop tuning, position loop tuning, fault thresholds, and brake timing all become part of the integration task.
An integrated robotic actuator combines some or all of the motor, gearbox, encoder, drive electronics, brake, temperature sensing, and communications interface. The attraction is obvious: fewer separate components, shorter wiring, compact packaging, and a defined interface between the actuator and robot controller.
The engineering tradeoff moves toward heat rejection, serviceability, firmware visibility, replacement strategy, and dependence on the actuator supplier.
The Robot Report‘s coverage of BLDC motors developed specifically for robot joints is one example of how motor packaging and performance requirements are increasingly considered together at the actuator level rather than as isolated motor components.
For any arm, the selection review should cover peak torque at every joint, holding torque at zero speed, brake requirements, backdrivability, and collision detection, torque estimation accuracy, and encoder placement. It should also cover gearbox efficiency, thermal soak, cable routing, mechanical compliance, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque disable or an equivalent safety function.
Match the controller to the mobile robot
BLDC motor control for mobile robots has a different emphasis because the wheels are both propulsion and contact with the environment.
A differential drive autonomous mobile robot (AMR) needs the two drive channels to track commanded velocities accurately enough for stable motion and navigation. Wheel speed feedback also contributes directly to odometry. Higher-resolution encoders become valuable when localization, synchronization, precise docking, or traction control demands more information than Hall commutation signals can provide.
Four-wheeled platforms introduce additional issues. Wheel speed matching, mechanical loading, steering or differential effects, and wheel slip can all influence control. Outdoor UGVs add water, dust, temperature changes, rough terrain, higher inertial loads, and longer periods of sustained power.
Battery behavior also changes the controller decision. Voltage sag under acceleration reduces the available electrical headroom, while regenerative braking can raise DC bus voltage. A controller designed around a nominal battery voltage therefore needs to be evaluated over the complete battery operating range rather than at one nominal value.
Thermal design is another difference. A drive enclosed inside a wheel or compact chassis may have limited airflow. The inverter, motor windings, bearings, connectors, and mechanical structure all become part of the heat path.
Harmonic Drive‘s servo-grade propulsion drive trains for AMRs illustrate this system-level relationship. Their characteristics include smooth travel, backdrivability, torque density, stiffness, and radial load support. The lesson is not that one transmission is appropriate for every AMR, but that propulsion control cannot be separated from the drivetrain.
Mobile manipulators make the distinction even more obvious. Desmasa’s MCR+ combined a robot arm and an AMR that shared one power and control architecture. The drive requirements of the base remained different from those of the arm, even though both ultimately contained electric actuators.
Evaluate current sensing and thermal behavior
Controller current ratings require careful interpretation. A datasheet may list continuous phase current, continuous bus current, peak phase current, peak current duration, RMS current, or a configurable current limit. These numbers are not interchangeable.
The motor’s thermal limit, inverter semiconductor limit, connector rating, cable rating, and battery capability can all be lower than a headline peak current specification. A controller advertised with a large peak current is therefore not automatically suitable for a motor that requires that current continuously.
BLDC.com provides a useful commercial example of the specification categories engineers encounter in controller selection. Its current controller catalog lists different input voltage ranges and current ratings across several controller families, while individual products describe interfaces and protection features.
Those specifications illustrate why engineers should compare voltage range, current definition, duration, feedback compatibility, and protection functions rather than simply comparing wattage.
The heat path must also be considered. Motor winding losses have to leave the motor through its structure and mounting arrangement. Power stage losses must leave the inverter through its enclosure, thermal interface, heat sink, airflow, or mounting structure. Thermal testing under the actual duty cycle is more informative than relying only on a short unloaded bench test.
Consider the communications and software layers
The motor controller is normally responsible for the fastest control loops. A robot controller does not need to calculate every PWM transition. Instead, the drive can execute current regulation and commutation locally while receiving higher level torque, velocity, or position commands.
Before selecting a drive, engineers should check CAN or CANopen support, EtherCAT support, RS 485 or UART, analog and PWM inputs, encoder interfaces, feedback update rates, command latency, fault reporting, firmware update procedures, parameter storage, multi axis synchronization, ROS 2 or ros2_control integration, and CiA 402 support where applicable.
CANopen’s CiA 402 profile standardizes functional behavior for servo drives and other motion control devices, including operating states and command/status structures. That can simplify interoperability when the selected hardware actually implements the required profile.
EtherCAT becomes attractive when synchronized multi axis motion and deterministic timing are central requirements. Its distributed clock architecture allows participating devices to synchronize their local timing.
ROS 2 integration is a separate consideration from the physical bus. Ros2_control represents robot hardware through command and state interfaces and provides a framework for connecting controllers to physical actuators. The controller manager also emphasizes deterministic control loop execution, showing why communication availability alone does not guarantee real time behavior.
Treat safety as an architecture, not a checkbox
A motor controller should be evaluated for overcurrent, short circuit, overvoltage, undervoltage, overtemperature, overspeed, encoder failure, Hall failure, phase loss, stall detection, brake control, communications loss, regenerative voltage rise, unintended restart, emergency stop behavior, and safe torque off where applicable.
These functions are not automatically equivalent to a complete safety architecture. Safety requirements depend on the robot category, risk assessment, operating environment, and system design.
For industrial robots, ISO 10218 1:2025 specifies safety requirements for industrial robots. ISO 13849 1:2023 addresses the design of safety related parts of control systems, including software. IEC 61800 5 2 addresses functional safety considerations for safety related adjustable speed power drive systems.
The important engineering distinction is that a controller having an overcurrent shutdown or temperature sensor does not, by itself, establish a certified safety function. The safety function has to be designed, validated, and integrated according to the applicable requirements.
A practical selection workflow
A useful motor controller selection process can be reduced to ten engineering steps.
- Step 1: Define the complete load and motion profile, including acceleration, deceleration, payload, terrain, gravity, and duty cycle.
- Step 2: Calculate continuous and peak torque at the motor shaft and, where applicable, at the joint or wheel.
- Step 3: Establish the required speed, acceleration, operating range, and regenerative braking conditions.
- Step 4: Define the control objective: speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction.
- Step 5: Select feedback according to the actual control objective and mechanical transmission.
- Step 6: Select six step, sinusoidal, or FOC control based on motion quality, speed range, torque requirements, and implementation constraints.
- Step 7: Check voltage, continuous and peak current, regeneration, thermal margins, and battery behavior.
- Step 8: Select the communication and software interfaces needed by the robot architecture.
- Step 9: Define safety behavior, fault response, braking, communication loss behavior, and restart conditions.
- Step 10: Validate the complete motor, drive, gearbox, sensor, brake, and robot controller as one system.
BLDC motor control selection decision table
Commissioning and validation
A controller should not move directly from a wiring diagram to production operation. First, verify phase order and encoder direction. Confirm Hall or encoder alignment and current sense polarity. Run the motor unloaded at reduced voltage where the hardware permits it, then compare commanded and measured speed.
Next, check position error and current behavior. Apply a controlled mechanical load and measure phase current and bus current. Monitor motor and inverter temperatures during acceleration, steady operation, and repeated cycles.
Regenerative braking deserves a dedicated test. Measure the DC bus during controlled deceleration and confirm that the battery, braking circuit, and controller remain within their operating limits.
Communication loss testing should verify what the drive actually does when commands stop arriving. Sensor disconnection tests should confirm fault detection and the resulting state. Overcurrent, thermal protection, emergency stop, and brake behavior should also be tested under controlled conditions.
Finally, repeat the important tests after thermal soak. A drive that behaves correctly for several minutes at room temperature may behave differently after the motor and inverter reach their operating temperatures.
For a robotic arm, these tests should be performed with the gearbox and representative mechanism installed. For a mobile robot, they should include the actual wheel, vehicle mass, battery, terrain, and representative duty cycle. A bench test of an unloaded motor validates only part of the system.
Engineer’s checklist
- What are the continuous and peak torque requirements?
- What is the required speed and acceleration range?
- Is the objective speed, torque, position, impedance, or traction control?
- Is Hall feedback sufficient, or is encoder feedback required?
- Is motor side feedback sufficient for the mechanical transmission?
- Does six step control provide adequate motion quality, or is FOC justified?
- Are voltage, current, regeneration, and thermal margins adequate?
- Does the communications interface meet latency and synchronization requirements?
- What happens during sensor failure, communication loss, braking, and emergency stop?
- Has the complete actuator been tested under the actual mechanical duty cycle?
Pulling together criteria to pick the right motor
The correct BLDC motor control architecture is determined by the control variable, mechanical transmission, feedback quality, duty cycle, thermal limits, energy system, safety architecture, and software integration.
For a simple mobile drive, a sensored six-step controller may provide an adequate combination of cost, robustness, and speed regulation. A demanding robotic joint may instead require encoder based FOC, nested torque, velocity, and position loops, and possibly output side feedback.
An outdoor mobile platform may need closed loop traction control, careful regenerative energy management, environmental protection, and thermal capacity that would be unnecessary on a small indoor robot.
The key decision is therefore not simply which BLDC motor controller has the right voltage or wattage rating. The useful question is whether the complete motor, inverter, feedback system, transmission, power source, communications layer, and safety architecture can produce the required behavior throughout the robot’s actual operating envelope.

candidato.titulo: AWS Will Run Its European Sovereign Cloud Without the Global Backbone for Several Hours
candidato.resumo: On October 24, AWS will operate its European Sovereign Cloud without a connection to the AWS Global Network backbone, with a team of EU residents and the region’s own hardware and software. AWS says neither of the two systems being severed is operation-critical, and practitioners are divided over whether the exercise answers the question customers are asking. By Steef-Jan Wiggers

texto_fonte:
On Saturday, October 24, AWS will cut its European Sovereign Cloud off from the AWS Global Network backbone for several hours. The region is expected to keep running. What that proves is a narrower thing than the argument now going on around it, and AWS says so itself.
Two systems come out. One is the Global Network backbone, the private network that moves operational data between AWS locations. The other is a dedicated channel for limited data transfers, switched off entirely. Traffic then falls back to the public internet over the region’s own links from European ISPs. Stéphane Israël, managing director of the AWS European Sovereign Cloud, says a team "composed entirely of EU residents working in the EU" will run it on the region’s own hardware and software, out of data centers in Brandenburg that hold a local in-EU copy of the source code. Customers may see short disruptions while routes converge at either end.
The caveat comes from AWS. Neither system is operation-critical. That is why the region survives without them. It is also why the region uses both every other day of the year. Data gets a sharper line. Customer content and customer-created metadata stay in the EU. Some operational data leaves. Israël writes that the exercise is built to line up with the EU Cloud Sovereignty Framework and Germany’s BSI C3A criteria, and that customers can put the results into their compliance packages. Regulators hear about it afterwards too. The post stops well short of claiming certification. It does not pretend the region runs isolated the rest of the year either.
None of that care has settled anything. Fadi Dasus, a senior cloud security architect, split the question in two:
Sovereignty on a US-owned cloud in the EU comes down to two areas. The technical one: does the service stop if the link to the US is cut? The legal one: can US law order it to hand over your data, or to stop serving you? If the test goes as planned, the first area is no longer entirely in American hands. The second still runs through the US parent. So, this is real progress for resilience. It just isn’t sovereignty.
Lars Larsson Lundsten, field CTO at Elastisys, which sells a European alternative to US cloud platforms, put it harder. "You can’t solve legal problems with technical solutions" he wrote, while calling the architecture a marvel of engineering. He also credited AWS with restraint, noting it is "extremely careful not to claim anything besides what this is able to actually prove."
The legal framing drew its own pushback. Commenter Roelf Zomerman argued that the CLOUD Act and the EU e-Evidence regulation both run through criminal investigations, with judges, provider evaluation and data limits attached, rather than working as a general power to demand data. Building your own, he added, or hosting with EU providers, "doesn’t automatically imply you are safe from these laws." Anders Bjørnestad, a principal consultant and AWS Community Hero, corrected a related assumption:
There are two aspects of this discussions. "Can someone get access to my data", and "can someone shut me off". What is tested here is the last part. The first part can be solved with encryption if you do it the right way. And all companies doing business in/with the US in some form are bound by US part of law, it is not only ownership that counts.
The hardest technical question came from a municipal IT manager rather than a vendor. Odd-Arne Haraldsen, who runs IT operations at Svenljunga Kommun in Sweden, called the design impressive, then asked what a few hours actually establishes:
How long can it actually operate independently? How long before systems fall out of sync? How long before authentication tokens, certificates, or licences expire? And how long before dependencies on external control planes begin to undermine that resilience? Redundancy is not the same as independence, and continued operation is not the same as sustained autonomy.
So the overclaiming charge misses. AWS has not stretched its evidence. The gap sits between what the exercise measures and what buyers keep asking. Take the obvious case. The post never says what happens to global services while the backbone is down. One commenter asked how IAM works when the region is cut off from the rest of AWS. Another said he could not picture DNS and internet routing holding up. The announcement addresses neither. Commenter Jarrod B. went at the audience question instead: the exercise "isn’t meant to appease legal purists; it’s designed to satisfy European risk officers and regulators." AWS hands the results to compliance teams, so he may be reading it right.
One exchange put the engineering in longer perspective. A commenter recalled a global AWS outage that appeared to show parts of AWS depending on us-east-1 and unable to run anywhere else. Lundsten gave ground in reply: if AWS has engineered that dependency away, its architecture is better for it.
AWS has given no launch date for the region. It calls the thing "a new, independent cloud for Europe." An update follows October 24.

candidato.titulo: Chip fab engineering game goes viral in Taiwan
candidato.resumo: A new 3D web game where you live 'A Day in the Life of a Semiconductor Wafer Factory Worker' has gone viral in Taiwan, where it was developed.

texto_fonte:
A new 3D web game where you live "A Day in the Life of a Semiconductor Wafer Factory Worker" has gone viral in Taiwan, where it was developed. Available in Chinese, English, and Japanese, Fab24hr is a work simulator where you play one of several semiconductor engineer roles in a blocky isometric 3D factory. Though the graphics might look basic, Taiwan’s TVBS news says that the game is so realistic that it resonates with fab workers but not always in a good way – some have likened it to "a horror game" or "prison" [machine translation].
If you head over to the Fab24hr site, the game UI loads pretty quickly and you are asked to input a character name and ‘Clock in.’ Then two game modes are presented. You can play the main story, dubbed ‘The life of a chip’ where you character works through 12 chapters shepherding a hearing-aid chip from the R&D line into the hands of an end user. In this mode your blocky fab worker character will simulate dealing with equipment failures, process anomalies, and production progress emergencies. You might also have to file reports about operational errors. Apparently there are three endings to this 12-chapter game, depending on your progress and decisions.
Another game mode is called ‘A day in the fab.’ Here you pick a factory location and role. For example, you can choose to be a Process Engineer. Your day started with the ETCH-03 semiconductor tool breaking, and “everyone is waiting for you to say what time it will be fixed.” Though this might sound like you’ve been thrown in at the deep end, if you pay attention to the handover from the previous shift, there should be clues to get you by. Technical terms are explained in the game so even those with no semiconductor industry experience should be able to ‘enjoy’ this escapade.
I briefly tested the game in my browser, where it ran without issues. It didn’t take long to understand why some Taiwanese fab veterans felt this simulator was kind of stressful, or even “super scary.” It isn’t the kind of free-time escapism I’m looking for.

candidato.titulo: Astronomers want your help finding 'missing' black holes in the Milky Way
candidato.resumo: A citizen science project is seeking volunteers to comb through NASA telescope data for telltale signs of the galaxy's hidden black holes.

texto_fonte:
Astronomers estimate that our home galaxy, the Milky Way, has churned out more than 10 million black holes over its 13-billion-year history. Yet so far, they have found only 70.
Now, a group of astronomers in the U.K. is trying to close that vast gap by enlisting the public. Their project, called Black Hole Hunters, is looking for volunteers with a computer and a few spare minutes to sift through troves of data gathered by a NASA space telescope. By flagging recognizable patterns that could point to a "missing" black hole, volunteers can help fast-track a search that would otherwise take years, the team says.
"You'll be narrowing down precisely where we need to point our telescopes next," project co-lead Adam McMaster, an astronomer at the University of Southampton in the U.K., said in a statement, "and you might be the one to discover a black hole."
Cosmic magnifying glasses
Black holes form when massive stars roughly 20 times heavier than our sun run out of fuel and collapse, leaving behind an abyss with gravity so immense that even light cannot escape. While invisible themselves, these cosmic behemoths reveal their presence by bending the light of nearby objects, and the Black Hole Hunters project is searching for one specific manifestation of this effect.
It happens thanks to the fact that massive stars often form in pairs, and a star can sometimes survive the violent supernova explosion that turns its companion into a black hole. When that happens, the two bodies continue to orbit each other. If such a duo aligns just right with Earth, the black hole will periodically pass directly between its companion star and our planet. And when it does, the black hole's gravity acts like a cosmic magnifying glass, bending and magnifying the star's light, causing it to briefly appear brighter to watchful telescopes.
To find these hidden giants, the project relies on data from NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite, or TESS. Although the satellite's primary mission is to hunt for planets beyond our solar system, its method of data collection — tracking tiny, continuous changes in a star's brightness over time — is ideally suited for identifying black hole magnification events, the project description notes.
"It's a simple task with no expertise required," McMaster said in the statement. "We will show volunteers examples of what to look for so all they have to do is recognise the right patterns."
Automated algorithms conduct a preliminary sweep of the TESS data, screening millions of potential stars for the most obvious black hole candidate locations, according to the project description. But, the researchers say, artificial intelligence struggles with the messy realities of the cosmos, such as stellar flares and the natural pulsations of stars that can trick the algorithms into false positives.
The human touch
That makes human volunteers a key part of the search. To keep errors in check, each graph is shown to multiple volunteers, and their answers are combined so that individual mistakes average out, according to the project's website.
"I can search for black holes on my laptop from my bedroom — and could make a real impact on real space science," Grace Clarke, an undergraduate student of physics and astronomy at the University of Southampton who's involved with the project, said in the same statement. "The data's easy to understand — it's just pattern recognition — and you don't need a degree in astronomy to read it."
The crowdsourced shortlist of promising signals lets astronomers aim follow-up observations at specific stars, such as precise measurements of whether a star is being tugged at by an unseen companion. Those measurements take time and are expensive, so a good shortlist helps researchers spend scarce telescope time wisely, the team says.
Since launching on the Zooniverse platform in October 2021, the project has attracted nearly 23,000 volunteers, who have completed more than 12 million classifications, according to its website.
Before turning to TESS, the team ran a similar search using data from SuperWASP, a ground-based survey that, like TESS, monitored stars for signs of planets from 2004 to 2016. Those results are still being analyzed and are expected to be published soon.
The team also plans to widen its search with observations from other instruments, including the European Space Agency's Euclid mission and NASA's recently launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
"With potentially thousands of new discoveries, we need all the help we can get," McMaster said in the statement.
Sharmila Kuthunur is an independent space journalist based in Bengaluru, India. Her work has also appeared in Scientific American, Science, Astronomy and Live Science, among other publications. She holds a master's degree in journalism from Northeastern University in Boston.

candidato.titulo: Quantum magic state cleanup cuts errors 40-fold in first successful hardware test
candidato.resumo: Qubits, the quantum equivalent of digital bits, are fragile and prone to errors. That makes building reliable quantum computers extremely difficult. One fix has been to use traditional magic state distillation, which filters out flaws, but it is extremely resource-intensive.

texto_fonte:
Quantum magic state cleanup cuts errors 40-fold in first successful hardware test
Paul Arnold
Author
Qubits, the quantum equivalent of digital bits, are fragile and prone to errors. That makes building reliable quantum computers extremely difficult. One fix has been to use traditional magic state distillation, which filters out flaws, but it is extremely resource-intensive.
Another potential solution is magic state cultivation, which cleans up a noisy magic state (a specially prepared quantum state that is needed for advanced calculations) directly inside a protected qubit. But this approach has never been tested successfully on real hardware.
However, in a first for quantum computing, Google Quantum AI researchers have demonstrated magic state cultivation on Willow, a superconducting processor, and it has cut errors dramatically.
Cleaning up noisy quantum states
The team first needed some errors to fix.
So, in their experiment, they encoded a noisy magic state across several physical qubits, spreading the quantum information over a small grid of qubits to protect it against errors.
Then, they tried to weed out the errors in the noisy state using helper qubits to scan the information for mistakes without destroying the delicate data itself.
If the checks caught any flaws, the system threw that attempt away and started over. If an attempt passed every test, the refined magic state was kept for further processing.
A dramatic drop in errors
The results, which are published in the journal Science, were striking. "Cultivation reduces the error by a factor of 40," the scientists wrote. And that yielded refined magic states with a fidelity of at least approximately 99.99% (a measure of how closely the prepared quantum state matches the intended state).
Checking such tiny levels of error required a new approach, so the scientists developed a checking method called kickback tomography. It is capable of detecting remaining errors using far fewer measurements than traditional techniques.
And the filtering was strict. Only about 8% of the initial attempts passed every check used to measure the state's fidelity.
The research team also transferred these cultivated magic states into a larger protective arrangement compatible with a surface code, a system designed to protect quantum information from errors. This suggests that the cleaned-up quantum states can be transferred into larger codes for future storage and use. "Overall, our grafting results show a proof-of-principle demonstration of a magic state escaping into an advantageous code."
The research addresses one of the major obstacles holding back quantum computing, which is the massive amount of extra equipment needed to create the special states for universal calculations. Cultivation helps by refining noisy states directly inside a protected qubit, potentially reducing the resources needed to produce them.
Next steps for this technology include scaling it up for larger quantum computers.

candidato.titulo: Official DLSS 5 running on unsupported games delivers up to 90% better performance than the leaked version
candidato.resumo: Nvidia's latest DLSS Neural Renderer, extracted from NBA 2K27 (again), is being tested on unsupported games and shows up to a 90% performance gain over the previous NR model.

texto_fonte:
A new version of DLSS 5 on NBA 2K27 was just released, and modders have already extracted it and are running it on unsupported games. Modders are comparing performance between the older and newer Neural Rendering (NR) model and found it up to 40% faster than the previous one.
While many are still experimenting with leaked and first-release builds, Renan Maniero has already extracted the new 310.9.16.0 DLSS NR build, letting other modders use it in unsupported games and compare performance. Gaming Optimized on X compared the new NR model to the old one and found massive improvements of up to 90% in The Witcher 3 running DLSS 5 natively.
Running a full NR model to modify your game's image is resource-intensive, just as LLMs require a lot of RAM; DLSS NR does, too. To improve performance, Nvidia made the AI model 24% smaller, using 20% less VRAM at 4K, and, according to Nvidia, processes its neural rendering workload up to 2x faster.
Typically, improving an AI model means increasing its parameters and size—in other words, giving it a bigger brain. However, because consumer GPUs have limited, non-upgradable VRAM, Nvidia can't improve by adding a bigger model; instead, the AI needs to become more efficient while reducing resource usage.
These comparisons were much easier than switching back and forth between updates, since the latest version still includes the older model as a preset. The new DLL has two Neural Rendering presets: Preset A is the old model, and Preset B is the newer model.
As with many other DLSS 5 experiments like those Valery Kryzhanovsky does, DLSS is injected into the graphics pipeline using RenoDX or OptiScaler, both of which let you tweak the DLL settings to get different results. To run DLSS NR on older RTX GPUs, the modding community also modified the runtime to support RTX 20-series GPUs, as the OptiScaler GitHub README notes.
Nvidia plans to release DLSS 5 to RTX 40-series GPUs, but there are no reports of it officially coming to RTX 30- or RTX 20-series cards; the modding community seems to have done it anyway.

candidato.titulo: Giving AI a “crystal clear” view of the materials world
candidato.resumo: New research can help AI models understand crystalline materials in 3D and reason about their properties.

texto_fonte:
In principle, artificial intelligence could make finding the right material for an application as simple as ordering dinner: Scientists would tell a large language model what they want, and it would serve them a perfectly designed crystal for the job.
Unfortunately, that approach doesn’t work well yet, and the problem comes down to data: Most materials consist of crystals, which are 3D periodic arrangements of atoms whose structures are stored in specialized formats, not the text streams that today’s large language models are trained on. The experimental literature is also heavily biased toward a few popular classes of crystals, making AI outputs skew toward those materials.
Now MIT researchers have created a multimodal AI model that tackles these problems. The model combines 3D atomic structures with natural language descriptions to create rich linguistic descriptions about the structures from experimental research papers and first-principles computational databases. The unified description outlines not just the chemical composition and structure, but also its properties, processing considerations, and potential applications, helping AI learn more about what makes materials impactful.
In a new paper in Nature Communications, the researchers showed their system could identify better material designs than models trained on text streams alone by allowing the model to “see” the atomic arrangements and bonding patterns. For example, when the researchers asked the model to identify materials suited for solid-state lithium-ion battery electrolytes, its top results included materials that had been independently identified as promising candidates. The researchers also showed their model learned geometric representations of material structures in ways text-only models could not.
“Structure is really at the heart of the materials science field,” says Ju Li, the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor in Power Engineering in the Department of Materials Science and Engineering (DMSE). “If you understand the structure, you can infer quite a lot about the properties and performance of materials. We wanted to build the connection between a material’s atomic structure and its properties and processing for the model.”
Joining Li on a paper about the model are Yang Jeong Park, first author and former MIT postdoc; Mayank Kumaran, a recent University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign computer engineering graduate; Chia-Wei Hsu SM ’26; and Elsa Olivetti, the Jerry McAfee (1940) Professor in Engineering in DMSE.
Getting models to see in 3D
Materials scientists are always on the hunt for new crystals that will lead to the products of the future. Over the last decade, AI has reshaped that process, proposing and designing new crystalline structures, which have highly ordered atomic structures and make up more than 90 percent of solid materials on Earth. Most of those models treat solid crystalline materials as 3D graphs.
The rise of large language models has given researchers another tool for innovation. But existing large language models rely heavily on text from published papers and books, limiting their knowledge of the physical world, since many potential crystal structures are stored in computational databases. Text-based models also lack understanding of visual geometry.
To overcome those challenges, the researchers decided to create a vision-language model for crystalline materials.
They trained a language model to create textual descriptions of crystal structures using an approach known as contrastive learning, in which models compare similar and dissimilar examples of structures and textual descriptions to achieve a unified understanding. This is similar to aligning the visual and language regions of the brain.
Following training, the researchers compared the predictions of two versions of the model: one trained on a dataset containing the AI-generated descriptions and the other trained on a dataset containing text from papers only. They found that the model trained on AI-generated descriptions successfully learned how to align geometric structures with text descriptions while the other did not.
“We wanted to create an AI model that works broadly across materials,” Li says. “That’s why we decided to synthesize narratives rather than rely solely on existing papers. We found when we used that narrative dataset, the models are better at predicting the function.”
Accelerating materials science
The researchers then showed their model could be given a natural language query describing a property and identify crystalline materials with that property, outperforming a baseline.
“There are sometimes these step changes within materials science around algorithmic integration toward useful tools, which the community uses to further advance the field,” Olivetti says. “This approach helps us see more deeply into three-dimensional structures and link structures to property and processing. I hope this can be one of those step changes.”
Li compares the model to AlphaFold, an AI model that links protein structures with function that has helped advance biological research and drug development.
The researchers believe their new approach can work with many crystalline materials, and they hope other material scientists will use it to accelerate their work.
“Being able to see a three-dimensional crystal and how its atoms are connected is super foundational,” Li says. “I think this will be useful to anyone who practices materials science.”
The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. Defense Threat Reduction Agency through the University Research Alliance; the U.S. Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency; and the National Research Foundation of Korea.

texto_fonte:
É possível fazer "remap" em carro elétrico?
Por Paulo Amaral |
O chamado remap automotivo (prática de reprogramar parâmetros eletrônicos para extrair mais potência e torque) já é comum em motores a combustão. Quando se trata de carros elétricos, porém, a técnica de "envenenar" o carro ainda é novidade e envolve custos mais altos.
Segundo o preparador automotivo Ricardinho ACF, que participou de um projeto experimental com o hatch elétrico Geely EX2 no Festival Interlagos 2026, é possível alterar a calibração para aumentar o desempenho sem comprometer os limites originais do motor. No entanto, o processo exige muito mais cuidado e investimento.
O especialista contou para a Quatro Rodas que a lógica de ajuste dinâmico é semelhante à dos motores a combustão, mas muda a forma como energia e calor são administrados. Em uso severo de curta duração, como uma bateria de drift de 10 minutos, é possível explorar picos de descarga elétrica para obter ganhos imediatos de torque. Porém, isso aumenta a temperatura do sistema, tornando o gerenciamento térmico o principal gargalo técnico.
O que muda no remap de elétricos
Assim como no motor a combustão o aumento da pressão do turbo exige intercoolers mais eficientes, no carro elétrico o remap demanda sistemas de refrigeração reforçados para suportar os picos de energia sem degradar as baterias ou danificar o motor.
Esse cuidado adicional explica por que o custo é maior: além da reprogramação eletrônica, é necessário investir em soluções de arrefecimento e componentes de alta tensão mais robustos. Ou seja, o remap em elétricos não é apenas uma questão de software, mas também de hardware.
Principais pontos sobre remap em elétricos
- É possível realizar remap em carros elétricos, mas exige maior investimento.
- O gerenciamento térmico é o maior desafio, já que o aumento de potência gera mais calor.
- Projetos experimentais já provaram a viabilidade, como o Geely EX2 modificado para o Festival Interlagos.
- O custo é superior ao de veículos a combustão, pois envolve ajustes em software e hardware.
- A prática ainda é restrita a preparadores especializados, sem aplicação em larga escala no mercado.
Se você se interessa por remap ou por "tunar" o carro, talvez queira entender melhor o que é permitido no tuning e o que é proibido na hora de "envenenar" seu carro; confira.
